_comment: Registry of off-the-shelf MCP servers the on-device agent can borrow.
Each entry is a config dict for harness/mcp_bridge.enable(), plus three
These are THIRD-PARTY servers. They hold your OAuth tokens, not us. See
ADDING-A-CONNECTOR.md in this folder for what that means and for the
migration path to first-party servers under mcp/servers/.

selftest.summary: Fake mailbox for testing the wiring. No credentials, no network.
setup: Nothing to set up. Verifies the bridge on a fresh machine:
python3 agents/8b/run_agent.py --mcp selftest --mcp-list
Draft mode should expose list/read/draft/modify and DROP send/reply/login.
notes: write_tools names modify_mail: it carries no write verb _WRITE_RE
recognizes, so the classifier already fails it closed to a write via
the unclassified default with no override at all. The override stays
as a clearer audit trail than that default, same reasoning as gmail's
modify_email and the ms365 family's write_tools.

gmail.summary: Gmail — read/search mail, create drafts. Draft mode drops send_email.
setup: Create an OAuth client (Desktop app) in Google Cloud, enable the Gmail API.
Save the client JSON as ~/.gmail-mcp/gcp-oauth.keys.json
Run once, interactively:  npx @gongrzhe/server-gmail-autoauth-mcp auth
That writes ~/.gmail-mcp/credentials.json, which the server reuses.
NOTE: this repo was archived March 2026 — still functional, but unmaintained.
It is the first candidate to replace with a first-party server.
notes: write_tools names modify_email, batch_modify_emails and
download_attachment. None of the three carries a write verb _WRITE_RE
recognizes, so the classifier already fails them closed to a write via
the unclassified default with no override at all. The override stays as
a clearer audit trail than that default. download_attachment also writes
to local disk, which is a write either way.

gcal.summary: Google Calendar — list/search events, free-busy, create and update events.
setup: Reuse the same Google Cloud OAuth client as gmail, and enable the Calendar API.
Point GOOGLE_OAUTH_CREDENTIALS at the client JSON (see env below).
First run opens a browser for consent and caches the token.

ms365-own.summary: Outlook mail and calendar, our own server. Fourteen tools, self-classifying.
setup: Our own first-party server. Install it into ITS OWN virtualenv, not
this one (see notes below for why):
cd ../ms365-mcp && python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -e .
Then sign in, against your own account:
export MS365_MCP_CLIENT_ID=<your Azure app registration id>
export MS365_MCP_TENANT_ID=organizations   # consumers for outlook.com
.venv/bin/python -m ms365_mcp --login
.venv/bin/python -m ms365_mcp --verify-login
verify-login calls Graph once. Do that before enabling this here: a
cached token can look healthy and still be refused, because a work or
school tenant can withhold consent for a scope the tools need, and
that only shows up on a real request.
Listing the connector works with no account at all, which is the
point of the Check button: it is the one connector whose effect
classes come from the server's own MCP annotations rather than from a
guess about its tool names, so it needs no read_tools or write_tools
overrides below.
notes: Runs under the SERVER'S OWN interpreter, not this repository's.
That is not a preference. The official MCP SDK on PyPI is called mcp,
so third-party servers should own their dependency set. Brick's local
selftest uses harness.mcp_selftest_server to avoid that package name,
but this does not make shared server dependencies safe in general.
A separate process should own its dependencies anyway; the process
boundary is the whole point of MCP.
Development wiring: the path assumes the sibling checkout and a POSIX
venv layout. Publishing the package would replace this with uvx.
No prefix: the tool names are already ours and already unambiguous
(list_messages, create_draft), and prefixing them twice would make
them longer for a model that reads every character of the tool list.
No allow list: fourteen tools is already inside the budget, which is
the whole design of that server.
send_draft is the only tool that transmits, so draft mode drops it and
the model cannot reach a person without --mcp-mode live.

ms365.summary: Outlook mail + calendar via Microsoft Graph. Draft mode drops send-mail.
setup: Run once, interactively, and call its 'login' tool to do the device-code flow:
npx @softeria/ms-365-mcp-server --preset mail,calendar
The token cache is reused after that, so the agent never sees the login.
Optional: set MS365_MCP_CLIENT_ID / MS365_MCP_TENANT_ID to use your own
Azure app registration instead of the server's built-in public client.
notes: arg_hints exist because these two tools take the WHOLE Graph entity under
a single 'body' argument — 25 top-level keys, with recipients and
start/end behind $defs $refs. Observed failures without them: 'body' sent
as a string, then contentType 'Text' rejected because the server's enum is
lowercase 'text'|'html' even though Graph's own docs capitalise it. The
shapes above were read off the live server's inputSchema, not the docs.
Measured, not guessed: `--mcp ms365 --mcp-list` against the real server
returns 69 tools even with --preset mail,calendar. That is far past what
an 8B can hold in an 8k context, so the allow list above cuts it to ten.
Widen it from the --mcp-list output, never from memory.
login/logout are dropped because the classifier reads them as harmless
(no write verb), which would let the model trigger a blocking device-code
prompt mid-run. A human logs in out of band; the agent never should.
write_tools covers copy-mail-message, dismiss-calendar-event-reminder and
snooze-calendar-event-reminder: none of the three carries a verb
_WRITE_RE knows, so the classifier already fails them closed to a write on
its own and would ask for confirmation with no override at all. The
override is kept anyway because a named entry here is a clearer audit
trail than relying on the unclassified default to land on the same
answer by coincidence.

ms365-personal.summary: Outlook mail + calendar for a PERSONAL account (outlook.com/hotmail).
setup: Log in once with the same authority the agent will use:
MS365_MCP_TENANT_ID=consumers npx @softeria/ms-365-mcp-server --login --preset mail,calendar
Then enter the code at https://www.microsoft.com/link (NOT login.microsoft.com/device).
Do NOT trust --verify-login: it reports 'Silent token acquisition failed'
even when the connection is fine. Test with a real call instead:
python3 agents/8b/run_agent.py --mcp ms365-personal --mcp-list
notes: See 'ms365' for why arg_hints are here: contentType is lowercase
'text'|'html', and the whole message goes under one 'body' argument. See
'ms365' too for why write_tools still names copy-mail-message,
dismiss-calendar-event-reminder and snooze-calendar-event-reminder even
though the classifier would fail them closed to a write on its own: the
override is a clearer audit trail than the unclassified default.
Use this, not 'ms365', for a personal Microsoft account. The server's own
auth.js carries the reason: as of June 2026 Microsoft rejects tokens issued
to personal accounts through the default 'common' authority, so the tenant
must be pinned to 'consumers'. Symptom if you get it wrong: the device page
bounces to localhost/callback with a missing 'response_type' error and no
token is ever cached.
The authority must match between login and runtime — hence the env here.

teams.summary: Microsoft Teams chat — list chats, read messages. Posting needs --live.
setup: Same server and same login as ms365, with --org-mode for work/school features.
Requires a work/school account; a personal Microsoft account has no Teams.
If your tenant restricts the server's built-in app, register your own Azure
app and set MS365_MCP_CLIENT_ID / MS365_MCP_TENANT_ID — this usually needs
a tenant admin to consent to the Chat.* delegated scopes.
notes: IN DRAFT MODE THIS IS READ-ONLY. Teams has no concept of a draft, so every
way to put a message in front of a person is a transmit tool and the bridge
drops all of them. Reading chats works; posting needs --mcp-live.
Running this alongside 'ms365' starts a second copy of the same server.
Use 'ms365-work' instead to get mail + calendar + teams in one process.

ms365-work.summary: One server covering Outlook mail, calendar and Teams chat (work account).
setup: Same login as ms365. Use this INSTEAD OF ms365 + teams, not alongside them.
notes: No allow list here on purpose — this preset spans three surfaces, so run
`--mcp ms365-work --mcp-list` against your own tenant and narrow it to the
tools you actually demo. Unfiltered it is well over 100 tools.
write_tools names copy-mail-message, dismiss-calendar-event-reminder and
snooze-calendar-event-reminder for the same reason as 'ms365': none of
the three carries a verb _WRITE_RE knows, so the classifier already fails
them closed to a write with no override, and the override is kept only
as a clearer audit trail than that default.
